title: Search — how to find things in the reader
html:
Search — how to find things in the reader

The reader ships a search panel that looks through the titles, the chapter outlines and the body text of every document in the folder. This page describes how to use it and what a query means; docs/design.md describes how the reader is built.

Opening the panel

The panel is not on the page by default. Ask for it with the Search documents button in the toolbar, or press Ctrl+F (Cmd+F on macOS). It goes away again on Escape, on a click anywhere outside it, or when you pick a result with the field's open gesture.

Typing a query

Every pause in typing is a query: the results list updates as you type, about a tenth of a second after your hand stops. There is no search button to press.

The scope button at the right edge of the field names the scope in force. A search starts in Local scope — the document you are reading. Pressing the button switches to Global scope, which reads every document the site holds; the choice lasts as long as the panel does. Switching the scope runs the query again at once.

In the pages format the whole-site text lives in one search.json next to the page, and the first global search fetches it — once; after that the answers are as instant as they are in the other formats. Searching the document you are reading never waits: that text arrived with the document itself. The first global search shows Loading… where the results will appear, and the answer replaces it when the corpus lands.

Reading the results

The list shows one row per place the query is found, not one row per document: each row carries the passage around a hit, with the hit emphasised, and the file it was found in. Rows are ordered by relevance — a hit in a document's title outranks one in a chapter heading, which outranks one in the body — and the hits of one document stay together.

Selecting is deliberate: click a row (or move with ↑/↓, Home/End) and the preview below the list shows the whole document with every place the query occurs marked, the selected one standing out. Opening the document is a firmer gesture: double-click the row, or press Enter, and the reader navigates to that document at that passage — the article opens with the query's occurrences marked the same way, the passage you picked standing out. A mark covers what you typed and no more: query instal and "installation" is marked over its first six letters alone, the tail of the word left unmarked. The marks are the arrival's, not the reading's: they go when you navigate on. A row whose match is in the title or the outline alone has no passage in the body to land on; that document opens at its top.

Query syntax

You typeWhat it finds
bearingThe whole word "bearing" and any word that begins with it ("bearings", "bearing housing"), in any case.
gear ratioDocuments where both words appear. Spaces separate words, and every word has to be found.
齿轮箱The three characters consecutively, as written. A text that holds only "齿轮" elsewhere and "箱" elsewhere is not a hit.
齿Any text holding the character — a single character is matched on its own.

The rules behind the table:

  • Case does not matter. Bearing, bearing and BEARING are the same query.
  • A word matches whole words and their prefixes. instal finds "install", "installation" and "instalment". This applies to words written in letters and digits; there is no fuzzy matching and no wildcards.
  • A multi-character CJK query is a phrase. Chinese (and the other Han scripts) is written without spaces, so the reader takes the characters you typed as the phrase you meant: what is found is where they appear together, in the order you typed them. To look for two separate ideas, put a space between them — 齿轮 箱体 — and each part is then matched on its own.
  • A single CJK character is its own query. One character has no phrase to preserve, so it is found wherever it occurs, inside longer words included.
  • Punctuation separates. Spaces, punctuation and symbols between two runs of characters break the phrase the same way a space does: gear.ratio is the two-word query gear ratio.

What the panel never does

  • It does not rank by position or count only: a hit in a title always leads, however early or late it sits in the body.
  • It does not search code blocks or diagram sources for highlighting: a hit inside one is still a real result in the list, and selecting it scrolls the preview to the block that holds it, but the preview leaves those subtrees as authored so a rendered diagram is never turned back into source. Inline code — a code span inside a line of prose — is ordinary text to the highlight, and its hits are marked like any other. Rows after an unmarked hit still land on their own places — the block holds the hit's place in the order, whether or not it is marked.
  • It does not hold on to your query: clearing the field (the clear button at the left of the scope button, or deleting the text) empties the list and the preview, and closing the panel forgets the query.
